--- Item 6 ---
id: fig_csc_anchoring
figure_type: data
title: CSC Anchoring Effect
caption: >-
  Candidate-Signature Consensus (CSC, vermilion) versus free consensus (FREE\_exact, blue) on development set E (354 rows:
  196 ERROR, 158 CORRECT; 144 sentences). (a) Error endorsement $e$, the rate at which peers endorse an erroneous candidate
  (ERROR rows): CSC raises it from 0.173 to 0.459 (arrow, $+0.286$, anchoring). (b) Correct-row divergence $d$ (CORRECT rows):
  CSC lowers it from 0.323 to 0.139 (arrow, $-0.184$, convergence). Lower is better in both (a) and (b), which show point
  estimates; the source reports no interval for $e$ or $d$. (c) Stratified AUROC for separating ERROR from CORRECT rows, with
  95\% CIs (bars) and chance at 0.5 (dashed): CSC 0.614 [0.493, 0.736] lies below FREE\_exact 0.770 [0.686, 0.844], c\_score\_align
  0.774 [0.682, 0.857] and p\_peer\_text 0.799 [0.700, 0.880] (grey). Giving peers the candidate's own symbols buys convergence
  on correct rows at the price of anchoring on errors, a net loss in discriminative power. This is a provisional negative
  on a completion-selected subset of E.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Side-by-side grouped bar chart with two panels. Left panel title: 'Error Endorsement (e)'. Right panel title: 'Correct-Row
  Divergence (d)'. Each panel has two bars: CSC (red) and FREE_exact (blue). Left panel values: CSC e=0.459, FREE e=0.173.
  Right panel values: CSC d=0.139, FREE d=0.323. Y-axis 0.0 to 0.5. Annotation arrow on left panel pointing from FREE bar
  to CSC bar labelled '+0.286 (anchoring)'. Annotation arrow on right panel pointing from FREE bar to CSC bar labelled '-0.184
  (convergence)'. Below both panels, a third mini-panel showing strat AUROC: CSC 0.614, FREE 0.770, c_score_align 0.774, p_peer_text
  0.799. White background, sans-serif font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  CSC raises error endorsement from 0.173 to 0.459 through anchoring while lowering divergence from 0.323 to 0.139. The net
  effect is negative: strat AUROC drops from 0.770 (FREE) to 0.614 (CSC).
figure_path: figures/fig_csc_anchoring_v0.pdf

  fraction of ERROR candidates endorsed by the peer majority, lower is better), correct-row divergence $d$ (amber; fraction
  of CORRECT candidates the peers disagree with, lower is better) and AUROC (green; whiskers are 95\% CIs). Tick labels give
  the regime and the data it was measured on, and grey badges give each regime's verdict. External vocabulary (SIG) reaches
  AUROC 0.954 with $e=0$, but it was measured on R\_COMP with a controlled, shared vocabulary, which is out of scope ($\dagger$:
  within-template AUROC; no CI reported). Candidate vocabulary (CSC) lowers $d$ to 0.139 but anchors peers into the candidate's
  errors ($e=0.459$), giving AUROC 0.614. This is a provisional negative on a 354-row completion-selected subset of development
  set E. Independent vocabulary (FREE, exact matching on the same 354 rows) keeps $e$ at 0.173 at the cost of $d=0.323$ (AUROC
  0.770). Gloss-gated filtering (GG, iteration 5, 2{,}672 rows of E) cuts $e$ to 0.081 but raises $d$ to 0.629 (AUROC 0.696)
  and fails its development gate g3. The CSC, FREE and GG AUROCs are stratified AUROCs on development set E, so SIG is not
  directly comparable with the other three.

  vocab)', 'GG (gloss-gated)'. Each column shows a flow: Sentence at top, arrow down to 'Peers translate using [source] vocabulary',
  arrow down to metric box. SIG column: e=0.0, d=0.260, AUROC=0.954. CSC column: e=0.459, d=0.139, AUROC=0.614. FREE column:
  e=0.173, d=0.323 (E); d_floor=0.402 (R_COMP). GG column: e=0.081, d=0.629, AUROC=0.696. Below each column a verdict badge:
  SIG='Best but requires ontology (out of scope)', CSC='Provisional negative (anchoring)', FREE='V0 shipped; rename unsolved',
  GG='Gate g3 FAIL (d too high)'. Colors: SIG column green-tinted, CSC column red-tinted, FREE column yellow-tinted, GG column
  orange-tinted. Arrows from candidate formula to CSC peers are red (indicating contamination path). White background, clean

aspect_ratio: '16:9'

### [21] HUMAN-USER prompt · 2026-09-25 17:15:43 UTC

```
I work on converting natural-language text into first-order logic (NL→FOL, autoformalization) with
LLM pipelines. Evaluation is the bottleneck. Correct FOL for a sentence is not unique — different
predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can
all be correct. Gold FOL annotations are rare and expensive. The metrics in use either need a gold
formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence to the gold) or only check that the output
parses. In my own pilot I used cheap structural metrics: whether a set of generated formulas loads
together without conflicts, whether predicate arities stay consistent, how many predicates are used
but never defined, and how similar the predicate sets are across reruns. Those measure stability and
composability, not whether a formula says what the sentence says.

Find new metrics for NL→FOL output quality. Operating situation: you are given a natural-language
sentence (or short passage) and a candidate FOL formalization produced by any system. There is no gold
formula, no ontology or controlled vocabulary, and no domain knowledge. The metric returns a score
that predicts whether the formalization is faithful to the text, and ideally which kind of error it
contains (quantifier or scope error, dropped or added condition, negation/polarity error, swapped
arguments, conflated or wrongly split concepts). Metrics may score a single formula or a set (several
samples for one sentence, or the formalizations of all sentences in one document). They must be
task-agnostic — usable for any NL→FOL setting, not tied to a domain, dataset or pipeline — and cheap
enough to run on every output (solver calls and small models are fine; a large-LLM judge per formula
only if shown to earn its cost).

Requirements:
- Keep the target fixed: the metric must predict faithfulness to the text. Detecting synthetic
  perturbations, parse validity, or run-to-run stability are not substitutes for that target.
- Validate against ground truth, never against the metric itself. Use public datasets with gold
  sentence-level FOL (e.g. FOLIO, MALLS, or others you find) to build a meta-evaluation set: real
  candidate formalizations from several different systems, plus controlled perturbations of gold
  formulas with known error types, labelled via prover-checked equivalence to gold. Handle two known
  problems: some gold annotations are wrong, and a candidate can be correct without being equivalent
  to the gold (different vocabulary or granularity). Estimate how often each happens and how it
  biases the labels. These datasets are public, so check whether LLM-based metrics benefit from having
  seen the gold.
- For each metric report: correlation with correctness at item and system level; sensitivity per error
  type; invariance under meaning-preserving rewrites (variable/predicate renaming, reordering,
  equivalent restatements); coverage — unparseable outputs are counted and reported, never silently
  dropped; and cost.
- Compare against baselines: parse/compile rate, round-trip (FOL→NL→compare) similarity,
  LLM-as-judge, sampling self-consistency, and the structural consistency metrics described above. A
  new metric matters only if it adds signal those don't.
- Report how each metric's reliability changes with sentence complexity (length, number of quantifiers,
  nesting depth, number of conditions and exceptions). Long, heavily conditioned sentences matter most
  to me.
- Negative results are welcome: if a family of metrics does not track correctness, show that clearly.

Out of scope: comparing grounded vs ungrounded generation (ontology vocabulary injected into prompts),
anything that depends on a particular ontology, and building a better NL→FOL translator. The
contribution is the measurement, not the translator.

Deliverables: reusable Python functions taking (text, fol) — or a set of such pairs — each with a
precise statement of what it measures; the meta-evaluation dataset with its labels; and the results.

I appended a pilot study of this problem with some metrics I already used but haven't verified. Just for reference.
```

(C) Cross-system consensus: collect translations of the same sentence from multiple independent systems, measure z3-equivalence between the candidate and the peer pool, and score disagreement [8]. Among non-equivalent parseable items, 21.9% are correct-but-not-equivalent (VOCAB or GRAN class).\n\n### 1.3 Experiment C: Cross-System Consensus\n\n[ARTIFACT:art_i3cVDxBp-USk]\n\nThe consensus metric collects translations of the same sentence from multiple independent LLM families, checks pairwise z3 equivalence, and scores each candidate by its disagreement with the pool. Total API spend was $1.52.\n\n#### Headline AUROCs (track L, ERROR vs CORRECT, n = 546, 249 errors)\n\n| Metric | AUROC | 95% CI | AUPRC |\n|-|-|-|-|\n| c_score (1 − eq_frac, all peers) | 0.866 | [0.821, 0.906] | 0.827 |\n| c_score (6 fresh peers only) | 0.872 | [0.830, 0.911] | 0.825 |\n| c_score (non-OpenAI peers) | 0.863 | [0.820, 0.903] | 0.808 |\n| c_score (2 Logic-LM peers only) | 0.753 | [0.701, 0.806] | 0.659 |\n| medoid depth | 0.722 | [0.673, 0.774] | 0.622 |\n| cluster entropy | 0.773 | [0.724, 0.820] | 0.691 |\n| SC-5 cheap (gpt-4.1-nano) | 0.725 | [0.669, 0.781] | 0.627 |\n| SC-5 same model | 0.716 | [0.632, 0.796] | 0.628 |\n| SC-5 entropy | 0.631 | [0.568, 0.693] | 0.539 |\n| Prediction set instability (SC) | 0.688 | [0.626, 0.750] | 0.602 |\n| Prediction set instability (pool) | 0.770 | [0.717, 0.821] | 0.721 |\n| FOL length | 0.527 | [0.470, 0.586] | 0.485 |\n| Misalignment (vocab) | 0.835 | [0.794, 0.876] | 0.821 |\n\n[FIGURE:fig_consensus_auroc]\n\nThe c_score achieves the highest AUROC in the iteration at 0.866. It beats SC-5 (the self-consistency baseline) by ΔAUROC = +0.140 [0.085, 0.197]. Cross-family consensus also exceeds sampling self-consistency in the related SAC3 framework [17], which uses semantic-aware cross-check consistency for hallucination detection in black-box LLMs. Using only the six fresh peer translations (not the three Logic-LM systems) gives 0.872, slightly higher than using all peers. Restricting to the two other Logic-LM systems drops the AUROC to 0.753, showing that diversity across model families is essential.\n\n\nThe misalignment score (0.835) is high because CORRECT items are by construction alignable to the gold in the labeller, so misalignment alone is a strong proxy for error. This does not generalise to settings without a shared vocabulary.\n\n#### RENAME rewrite invariance: failure\n\nUnder predicate renaming (replacing predicate names with WordNet synonyms or nonce names), the c_score false-alarm rate is 96% (100% for constant-only renaming). This is expected and fundamental: two formulas with different predicate names are not z3-equivalent, so any rename breaks the equivalence check. The consensus metric is invariant to rewrites that preserve z3 equivalence (reordering, De Morgan, contrapositive) but not to vocabulary changes.\n\n#### Blind-spot analysis\n\n38% of ERROR items are z3-equivalent to the medoid (the most popular peer formula). This places a ceiling on recall of approximately 62%. The blind-spot rate is 5% for polarity errors and 57% for structural errors.\n\n#### Cost\n\nThe peer pool costs $0.0015 per sentence (6 peers via API). Total experiment spend: $1.52. z3 pairwise equivalence checking is free.\n\n### 1.4 Experiment D: Disguised Judge and Baselines\n\n[ARTIFACT:art_elDZY26Pu6GD]\n\nThis experiment establishes the bar: every baseline metric and every judge variant on the same shared screen, scored with nonce-disguised sentences to control for memorisation. The local Qwen3-8B judge achieves AUROC 0.757 (disguised), comparable to the API flash-lite judge at 0.777.\n\n### 1.5 Iteration 1 Summary\n\nThe four candidates and the bar:\n\n| Method | AUROC | 95% CI | n | Cost/item | Rewrite flip rate |\n|-|-|-|-|-|-|\n| c_score (consensus) | 0.866 | [0.821, 0.906] | 546 | $0.0015/sent | 96% (RENAME) |\n| S4 baseline combo | 0.817 | [0.762, 0.867] | 524 | varies | varies |\n| **Bar: judge_cheap_disg** | **0.777** | **[0.720, 0.827]** | **524** | **$0.00004** | **0.39** |\n| FOL-Triage fused | 0.759 | [0.695, 0.825] | 477 | $0.0002 | 0.013 |\n| rt_nli_min | 0.710 | [0.648, 0.769] | 524 | $0.00001 | 0.31 |\n| L1 lint | 0.508 | [0.499, 0.519] | 477 | $0 | 0.0 |\n| Pilot structural | 0.50-0.53 | n/a | 524 | $0 | n/a |\n\n[FIGURE:fig_summary_comparison]\n\n**What iteration 1 established:**\n\n1. The cross-system consensus metric (c_score = 1 − eq_frac) achieves the highest AUROC at 0.866, beating SC-5 by +0.140. It requires peer translations from multiple model families and is fundamentally non-invariant to predicate renaming (96% FA under RENAME).\n\n2. The disguised cheap judge sets the bar at AUROC 0.777. The S4 combination of all cheap features reaches 0.817 (+0.039, not significant). The frontier judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) adds nothing significant over the cheap judge under solver labels; under panel labels the advantage strengthens (+0.166, p < 0.001).\n\n3. FOL-Triage achieves AUROC 0.759, below the bar. Its primary value is invariance: the fused flip rate under meaning-preserving rewrites is 0.013, compared to 0.29-0.49 for judges. However, the fused false-alarm rate on CORRECT items is 0.194, exceeding the 0.10 calibration target.\n\n4. L1 lint does not transfer from human annotation errors to LLM outputs. The pilot structural metrics are null. Round-trip NLI is 0.067 below the judge.\n\n5. The evaluation labels are noisy: 58.8% of track-L \"errors\" are pure ADD+DROP (likely vocabulary mismatches). Iteration 2 will re-evaluate under panel-adjudicated labels from the development set.\n\n6. No contamination was detected for any LLM-based metric.\n\n**What remains for iteration 2:** (a) Re-evaluate all candidates under adjudicated labels from Artifact E. (b) Compute the paired ΔAUROC between FOL-Triage and the disguised judge on shared items. (c) Test whether combining the consensus metric with FOL-Triage or the judge produces a significant improvement. (d) Confirm on the development set.\n\n## Iteration 2\n\n### 2.1 Strategy\n\nIteration 2 has three goals: (i) confirm iteration 1's ordering on the development dataset E under both the solver labels (R_AB, R_A) and panel-adjudicated labels (R_ADJ); (ii) test whether fusing the consensus signal (PEER) with text-based checks (TEXT = L2-bow + L3) improves over each alone; and (iii) construct a typed perturbation suite (PERTURB) for controlled sensitivity testing.\n\nThe pre-registered bar for this iteration is the flash-lite judge on disguised sentences, with the local Qwen3-8B judge as fallback if the API is unavailable. The shared OpenRouter key hit its daily limit at 18:00 UTC on 2026-09-23, before the development-set experiment completed, and did not recover before the run deadline. The flash-lite bar is therefore UNTESTABLE on E; the fallback local judge (Qwen3-8B, rubric B, greedy; screen AUROC 0.757 vs 0.777 for flash-lite) is the labelled secondary bar for all rows reported below.\n\n### 2.2 Experiment 5: PEER+TEXT on development dataset E\n\n[ARTIFACT:art_TaxJRnPcJMuZ]\n\nPEER+TEXT is a logistic fusion of the consensus signal (c_score with shared-vocabulary alignment, denoted c_score_align) and the text-based FOL-Triage layers (L2-bow, L3 questionnaire). API spend was $0 (all components ran on CPU and the local GPU; no OpenRouter calls completed).\n\n#### Name-free alignment: failed the pre-registered screen gate\n\nA name-free variant of the consensus metric (graded clause consensus, g_score) was pre-registered as the primary PEER signal. It matches formula clauses by structural role without relying on shared predicate names, using anchored-cost assignment and Murty k-best matching. Under the pre-registered selection rule, both name-free variants (NF-pure and NF-anchored) failed the screen gate: for both, more than 10% of AGREE track-L CORRECT items tie at g = 1, making the deterministic false-alarm threshold degenerate (ROLE_PERMUTE recall = 0).\n\nA post-hoc analysis with fractional tie-breaking showed this failure was a threshold-tie artefact. NF-anchored passes both gates under fractional scoring (RENAME FA 0.074, ROLE_PERMUTE recall 0.771); NF-pure still fails ROLE_PERMUTE (recall 0.186). The NF-anchored fusion was fitted post-hoc and applied to E as a labelled sensitivity analysis. (d) Run the consensus metric on a fresh dataset (outside FOLIO/MALLS) to test domain transfer.\n\n## Iteration 4\n\n### 4.1 Strategy\n\nIteration 4 tests one new idea and builds infrastructure for confirmation. The idea is Candidate-Signature Consensus (CSC): instead of having peers translate independently (FREE) or from a shared external vocabulary (SIG), CSC feeds each peer the candidate formula's own predicate symbols and asks it to translate using those symbols. If the candidate is correct, the peers should converge on an equivalent formula; if it is wrong, they may either reject the candidate's vocabulary or be anchored into reproducing its error. CSC is tested on development set E (T6-E) and on the PERTURB suite (T6-P). The CSC prediction: cueing peers with the candidate's own symbols should give a lower d without a higher e; eval 3's pre-registered d_floor (instrument bracket 0.396–0.415, no-anchoring oracle floor 0.385) was the yardstick; stopping rule: CSC is dropped if G1 or G2 fails.\n\nPre-registered gates (verbatim from `prereg_csc_E.json`): G1: \"d(c_csc > 0.5 | R_AB CORRECT) ≤ 0.35 AND the words slope of GEE d ~ z(words) + z(n_conditions) among CORRECT rows has CI including 0 or entirely < 0\". G2: \"stratified AUROC(CSC) ≥ stratified AUROC(c_score_align) − 0.01 on R_AB AND pooled AUROC(CSC) > AUROC(c_score_align) on L25 (point estimates; the L25 paired CI is reported whatever its sign)\". G3-E: \"FA(c > 0.5) on RENAME_SYN CORRECT rows ≤ base FA (same rows, CSC-OWN) + 0.05 (point estimate; CI reported); NONCE reported as the stress boundary, not gated\". G5: \"FULL cost per candidate (sum of its peer calls, dedup-apportioned) ≤ $0.002\".\n\nActual spend: exp 9 $0.108, exp 10 $0.0000088, dataset 4 $0.241, dataset 5 $0, eval 3 no ledger (CPU only). [4] found that approximately 42% of entries in both datasets contain incorrect FOL formalisations, with additional ambiguity rates of 17.8% (FOLIO) and 51% (MALLS). [5] evaluate n-gram, graph, embedding, and LLM-based metrics on controlled FOL perturbations, finding that no single metric is sensitive to all perturbation types. Smatch++ is the most sensitive to quantifier changes, while BL-score responds most to negation. Their work measures sensitivity to synthetic perturbations; ours measures faithfulness prediction on real LLM outputs with noisy labels.\n\n**NL-FOL error taxonomies.** Thatikonda et al. [6] propose a verification pipeline with a 28-category error taxonomy. Brunello et al. [4] classify errors into semantic and structural categories. Our typed repair operators (NEG, REV, QUANT, RESTR, CONN, MOVE, DROP, ADD, SWAP, BIND, SCOPE, UNGLUE) follow the same tradition but are derived from z3 equivalence-class differences rather than manual annotation.\n\n**Factuality metrics.** FRANK [11] defines a typology of factuality errors in abstractive summarisation and evaluates correlation of automatic metrics with human judgments. QuestEval [13] uses question generation and answering to assess factual consistency. QAGS [12] similarly generates questions from a summary and checks whether the source answers them the same way. Our L3 questionnaire layer is closest to this family: it generates structured questions from the text and checks the formula's answers via z3, rather than using another LLM.\n\n**Round-trip and self-consistency.** Amrollahi et al. [7] propose verbalising a formal statement back to natural language and checking consistency, reporting high accuracy on mathematical autoformalization. Li et al. [8] use symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency for Lean/Isabelle autoformalization. Our round-trip baseline follows the same pattern but achieves only AUROC 0.710 on NL-FOL, below the LLM judge.\n\n**Monotonicity and polarity.** SyGNS [14] tests monotonicity reasoning in NLI models. Udep2Mono [15] computes monotonicity profiles from Universal Dependencies. Our L2 role-aware layer attempted to use monotonicity-aware comparisons but achieved AUROC 0.557, a negative result.\n\n**Counter-interpretation methods.** CLOVER [9] generates counter-interpretations to test logical validity via an LLM oracle. Our consensus approach is related in spirit: it uses multiple independent translations as implicit counter-proposals, but relies on z3 equivalence rather than LLM-generated counterexamples.\n\n**Cross-check consistency.** SAC3 [17] detects hallucinations in black-box LLMs by sampling diverse perturbations of a query and checking consistency across answers. Our cross-system consensus metric uses a similar principle: disagreement among independent translations signals error. It operates on FOL equivalence rather than textual similarity, and uses multiple model families rather than perturbations of a single model. Our approach differs in that we use no learned alignment model: the consensus signal relies on z3 equivalence among independent translations, and the text-based signal uses deterministic checks and a prompted questionnaire. FormalAlign targets mathematical theorem proving, where the target language has a type checker; NL-FOL has no such verifier, making gold-free evaluation harder.\n\n**Vacuity detection.** Kupferman and Vardi [16] formalise vacuity in temporal logic model checking. Our L1 lint layer includes a vacuity check (detecting formulas where a subformula can be replaced by its negation without changing the truth value), adapted from their framework.\n\n**Cross-model translation confidence.** Bayless et al. [19] apply the same score form as c_score—the share of k independent LLM translations that entail a candidate—to NL-to-SMT translation, using a fixed schema and downstream QA accuracy as the label. It is the closest methodological precedent to our cross-family consensus metric, but operates on a fixed shared schema (removing the rename tradeoff) and evaluates against downstream task labels rather than z3-reference faithfulness labels. This label-target reversal illustrates that meta-evaluation results depend on whether labels measure solver equivalence or human intent. Our evaluation uses both: solver labels (R_AB) and panel-adjudicated labels (R_ADJ, dropped in iteration 2 for gate failure).\n\n**Self-consistency for formal translation.** SCP-NL2TL [22] evaluates single-model self-consistency vs a judge vs back-translation for NL-to-temporal-logic translation, reporting that SC AUROC rises with difficulty tier. Vossel et al. [24] map predicates by normalised Levenshtein distance (threshold ≤ 0.6) before equivalence checking. Our aligner-based consensus (c_align) uses a similar principle but through z3 equivalence of aligned formulas. Chen and Avizienis [25] noted that \"faulty but identical results (due to missing logic) may outvote correct results\"—precisely the endorsement failure mode we measure (e = 0.124 on E, 0.459 under CSC). \documentclass[11pt,letterpaper]{article}

\title{Gold-Free Faithfulness Metrics for NL-to-FOL Translation}
\author{Internal Research Report}
\date{September 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Translating natural language into first-order logic (NL-FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning pipelines, yet evaluating whether a candidate formula faithfully captures a sentence's meaning remains an open problem. Gold FOL annotations are expensive, non-unique, and unreliable: approximately 42\% of entries in both FOLIO and MALLS contain incorrect formalisations. This report investigates gold-free metrics that predict faithfulness to the text given only a sentence and a candidate formula, with no reference formula, no ontology, and no domain knowledge. Over five iterations, we screen four metric families (FOL-Triage, round-trip verification, cross-system consensus, and LLM judges), construct development and confirmation datasets, and quantify a fundamental rename tradeoff. The cross-family consensus metric (c\_score\_align) achieves stratified AUROC 0.742 on a 700-sentence development set, beating the best cheap LLM judge (0.641) by +0.101 [+0.053, +0.145]. On controlled-vocabulary composed sentences, it reaches within-template AUROC 0.954 with zero error endorsement. The rename tradeoff---vocabulary dependence as the central unsolved problem---remains open: any renaming of predicates breaks the consensus signal (RENAME\_NONCE false-alarm rate 0.765), and no name-free variant simultaneously achieves low rename FA and high discrimination. All confirmation arms were budget-stopped before reaching testability.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents
\newpage

%% ============================================================
\section{Framing}
%% ============================================================

Translating natural language into first-order logic (NL-FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning pipelines~\citep{Pan2023}, yet evaluating whether a candidate formula faithfully captures a sentence's meaning remains an open problem. Gold FOL annotations are expensive, non-unique, and unreliable: \citet{Brunello2026} found that approximately 42\% of entries in both FOLIO~\citep{Han2022} and MALLS~\citep{Yang2023malls} contain incorrect formalisations. Existing metrics either require a gold formula (exact match, prover-checked equivalence) or only verify that the output parses~\citep{Thatikonda2025, Thatikonda2024}. The user's own pilot study used structural consistency checks (arity agreement, predicate-set overlap across reruns, joint satisfiability) that measure stability but not whether a formula says what its sentence says.

This run investigates gold-free metrics that predict faithfulness to the text given only a sentence and a candidate formula, with no reference formula, no ontology, and no domain knowledge. The evaluation is a meta-evaluation: we build a labelled set of (sentence, formula) pairs from public benchmarks whose gold has been audited, and measure each metric's ability to discriminate correct translations from errors.

%% ============================================================
\section{Iteration 1}
%% ============================================================

\subsection{Strategy}

The iteration screens four candidate metric families head-to-head on a frozen evaluation set, with a disguised cheap LLM judge as the bar to beat.

\textbf{Candidates.} (A)~FOL-Triage, a three-layer cascade: L1 (formula lint: deterministic formula smells), L2 (text accounting: bag-of-words and role-aware coverage), and L3 (role questionnaire: a small LLM reads the text and z3 reads the formula; their structured answers are compared). (B)~Round-trip verification: verbalise the formula back to natural language and compare to the original via NLI or embedding similarity~\citep{Amrollahi2026}. (C)~Cross-system consensus: collect translations of the same sentence from multiple independent systems, measure z3-equivalence between the candidate and the peer pool, and score disagreement~\citep{Li2024}. (D)~Disguised cheap judge and baselines: an LLM judge, structural pilot metrics, and round-trip features evaluated on nonce-disguised sentences to control for memorisation.

\textbf{Evaluation set.} The frozen screen uses Logic-LM~\citep{Pan2023} released outputs on FOLIO validation: three LLM systems (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, text-davinci-003) producing 796 items. Track~L contains LLM outputs labelled by z3 equivalence to corrected gold~\citep{Brunello2025}; track~H contains the 294 original human gold formulas, of which 57 are errors according to the corrected labels.

\textbf{Decision rule.} A candidate must achieve AUROC $\geq$ 0.65 on track~L (ERROR vs CORRECT), with coverage $\geq$ 90\%, rewrite false-alarm rate $\leq$ 10\% per rewrite family, and cost $\leq$ \$0.002 per item.

\textbf{Development dataset~E.} A separate 700-sentence, 8,507-row development set was constructed from FOLIO training premises, MALLS training long/conditional/exception strata, and FOLIO curated conclusions, each translated by 9 LLM families plus ccg2lambda plus GPT-4 gold. Labels were assigned by z3 equivalence to audited gold, with contested cases adjudicated by a three-member panel (Claude Haiku-4.5, GLM-4.6, Kimi-K2). The dataset contains 1,750 CORRECT, 5,005 ERROR, 1,086 UNPARSEABLE, 276 UNRESOLVED, and 390 CONTESTED items. Cost: \$9.83 in API calls.

\subsection{Experiment A: FOL-Triage}

FOL-Triage was evaluated on the frozen screen with Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite as the primary LLM for L3. Total API spend was \$0.29.

\subsubsection{L1 lint: a negative result on LLM outputs}

L1 flags formulas with deterministic smells (existential implication, free variables, arity clashes, vacuity, trivial formulas, dangling predicates). On track~L, the true positive rate is 2.0\% at a false positive rate of 0.4\%, giving AUROC 0.508. This is a negative result: L1 lint does not transfer from human annotation errors (where it is effective, AUROC 0.655) to LLM outputs.

\subsubsection{RENAME rewrite invariance: failure}

Under predicate renaming, the c\_score false-alarm rate is 96\% (100\% for constant-only renaming). This is expected and fundamental: two formulas with different predicate names are not z3-equivalent, so any rename breaks the equivalence check.

\subsubsection{Blind-spot analysis}

38\% of ERROR items are z3-equivalent to the medoid (the most popular peer formula). This places a ceiling on recall of approximately 62\%. The blind-spot rate is 5\% for polarity errors and 57\% for structural errors.

\subsubsection{Cost}

The peer pool costs \$0.0015 per sentence (6 peers via API). Total experiment spend: \$1.52.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.85\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_summary_comparison_v0.pdf}
  \caption{Iteration 1 summary comparison. Consensus leads at AUROC 0.866, followed by the S4 baseline combination (0.817) and the disguised cheap judge bar (0.777). FOL-Triage (0.759) is below the bar but has the lowest rewrite flip rate (0.013).}
  \label{fig:summary_comparison}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key findings:}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The cross-system consensus metric (c\_score = 1 $-$ eq\_frac) achieves the highest AUROC at 0.866, beating SC-5 by +0.140. It requires peer translations from multiple model families and is fundamentally non-invariant to predicate renaming (96\% FA under RENAME).
\item The disguised cheap judge sets the bar at AUROC 0.777. The S4 combination reaches 0.817 (+0.039, not significant). The frontier judge adds nothing significant over the cheap judge under solver labels; under panel labels the advantage strengthens (+0.166, p $<$ 0.001).
\item FOL-Triage achieves AUROC 0.759, below the bar. Its primary value is invariance: the fused flip rate under meaning-preserving rewrites is 0.013, compared to 0.29--0.49 for judges.
\item L1 lint does not transfer from human annotation errors to LLM outputs. The pilot structural metrics are null. Round-trip NLI is 0.067 below the judge.
\item The evaluation labels are noisy: 58.8\% of track-L ``errors'' are pure ADD+DROP (likely vocabulary mismatches).
\item No contamination was detected for any LLM-based metric.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Iteration 2}

\subsection{Strategy}

Iteration 2 has three goals: (i) confirm iteration~1's ordering on the development dataset~E under both the solver labels (R\_AB, R\_A) and panel-adjudicated labels (R\_ADJ); (ii) test whether fusing the consensus signal (PEER) with text-based checks (TEXT = L2-bow + L3) improves over each alone; and (iii) construct a typed perturbation suite (PERTURB) for controlled sensitivity testing.

The pre-registered bar is the flash-lite judge on disguised sentences, with the local Qwen3-8B judge as fallback. The shared OpenRouter key hit its daily limit before the development-set experiment completed, making the flash-lite bar UNTESTABLE on E.

\subsection{Experiment 5: PEER+TEXT on development dataset E}

PEER+TEXT is a logistic fusion of the consensus signal (c\_score\_align) and the text-based FOL-Triage layers (L2-bow, L3 questionnaire). API spend was \$0.

The paired $\Delta$AUROC of PEER+TEXT minus the local judge is +0.078 [0.043, 0.112] on R\_AB pooled (DeLong p $<$ 0.0001). On the long pool, the gap widens to +0.115 [0.075, 0.157].

The stratified AUROC (pairing only within complexity strata) shows PEER+TEXT at 0.753 and c\_score\_align at 0.741, a difference of +0.011 [$-$0.012, 0.038], not significant. The TEXT layers add no significant discriminative power over c\_score\_align alone once the stratum-composition confound is removed.

\subsubsection{Mechanism predictions}

\textbf{P1 (PEER catches COVERAGE errors that TEXT misses, and vice versa).} At matched false-alarm rate 0.10: PEER has higher recall than TEXT on COVERAGE errors (+0.093 [0.046, 0.147]), and TEXT has higher recall on PEER\_ENDORSED errors (+0.103 [0.051, 0.171]). Verdict: INCONCLUSIVE.

\textbf{P2 (PEER and TEXT error rankings are uncorrelated).} Spearman correlation between PEER and TEXT among errors is 0.294 [0.224, 0.365]. Verdict: REFUTED.

\textbf{P3 (PEER+TEXT advantage grows with sentence complexity).} The logistic interaction term is $-$0.023 [$-$0.228, 0.185], consistent with no interaction. Verdict: INCONCLUSIVE.

\textbf{P4 (PEER+TEXT is more invariant to meaning-preserving rewrites than judges).} RENAME FA: fused 0.385, local judge 0.683. Verdict: REFUTED (c\_score\_align drives most of the FA at 0.859).

\subsection{Iteration 2 Summary}

\begin{enumerate}
\item PEER+TEXT achieves AUROC 0.790 [0.75, 0.82] on development dataset E (R\_AB pooled, n = 2686), beating the local judge by +0.078 [0.043, 0.112] (DeLong p $<$ 0.0001).
\item Fusion does not significantly beat c\_score\_align alone. The stratified AUROC difference is +0.011 [$-$0.012, 0.038].
\item The name-free consensus variant (NF-anchored) failed the pre-registered screen gate due to a threshold-tie artefact.
\item Under adjudicated labels, FOL-Triage fused rises from 0.770 to 0.868. The c\_score drops from 0.849 to 0.779.
\item The frontier judge advantage is large under adjudicated labels (+0.166 AUROC, p $<$ 0.001).
\item All 57 reviewer-audited numbers from iteration 1 reproduce exactly (57/57 MATCH).
\item The PERTURB suite (4,234 typed mutants + 868 controls, 12 operator types) is complete.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Mechanism predictions (T4)}

\item \textbf{T5}: c\_align RENAME\_NONCE FA 0.765; c\_nf 0.132 but SWAP recall 0.512.
\item \textbf{T4}: M4 CONFIRMED (k95 = 3). M3 INCONCLUSIVE.
\item 48/48 numerical claims verified.
\item Iteration-3 API spend: \$4.33.
\end{enumerate}

%% ============================================================
\section{Iteration 4}
%% ============================================================

\subsection{Strategy}

Iteration 4 tests Candidate-Signature Consensus (CSC): instead of having peers translate independently, CSC feeds each peer the candidate formula's own predicate symbols and asks it to translate using those symbols. In parallel, the iteration constructs the E2 confirmation dataset (550 fresh sentences) and runs a vocabulary-analysis evaluation (T8).

\subsection{Experiment 9: CSC on development set E --- provisional negative result}

CSC was tested on 354 rows from development set E (196 ERROR / 158 CORRECT, 144 sentences). API spend: \$0.108.

\subsubsection{Anchoring: the core finding}

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{CSC anchoring effect.}
\label{tab:csc_anchoring}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Component & CSC & FREE\_exact (matched) \\
\midrule
e (error endorsement) & 0.459 & 0.173 \\
d (correct-row divergence) & 0.139 & 0.323 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

CSC dramatically lowers d but raises e from 0.173 to 0.459: nearly half of all errors are endorsed by peers anchored into the candidate's vocabulary.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.85\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_csc_anchoring_v0.pdf}
  \caption{CSC anchoring effect. CSC lowers correct-row divergence (d: 0.139 vs 0.323) but raises error endorsement (e: 0.459 vs 0.173). The net effect is negative: strat AUROC 0.614 vs FREE 0.770.}
  \label{fig:csc_anchoring}
\end{figure}

%% ============================================================
\section{What We Have Learned So Far}
%% ============================================================

The cross-family consensus metric (c\_score\_align) is the strongest gold-free faithfulness signal found in this investigation. On development set E, it achieves stratified AUROC 0.742, beating the best cheap LLM judge (0.641) by +0.101 [+0.053, +0.145]. On R\_COMP SIG (the out-of-scope controlled-vocabulary condition), it reaches 0.954 within-template AUROC with zero error endorsement. Three peer families suffice for 97\% of full-pool performance (M4 confirmed: k95 = 3; by words tercile k95 = 2/3/5).

The mechanism is clear: errors scatter across z3-equivalence classes while correct translations cluster. The consensus signal degrades with sentence length (NET +0.401 on development E, driven by divergence d), meaning longer sentences need more peers and the metric becomes less reliable precisely where it matters most.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.85\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_vocabulary_source_v0.pdf}
  \caption{The vocabulary source problem. c\_align RENAME\_NONCE FA is 0.765 on development E and 1.0 on E2: any renaming of predicates breaks the consensus signal. The GG checker reduces MEANING\_RENAME endorsement from 0.502 (V0) to 0.224 but fails the development gate (strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742) because the gloss gate rejects too many legitimate predicate mappings.}
  \label{fig:vocabulary_source}
\end{figure}

Iteration 5 attempted confirmation on three fronts, and all three were blocked by the run-wide budget (\$7.00). E2-A produced one testable cell: V0 reaches 0.916 on ProverQA-derived sentences with trusted gold, but only 0.443 on the L25 long-sentence stratum (near chance). E2-B's exploratory results (V0 0.737 vs flash-lite 0.496, $\Delta$ +0.208) favour consensus on long sentences with unaudited labels, but the label-coupling diagnostic shows part of the advantage comes from shared gold-equivalent peers. R\_COMP FREE's provisional results show c\_align 0.801 vs judge 0.584 ($\Delta$ +0.217) under ERROR\_CERT vs MAPPED labels, with consensus carrying most of the signal in nesting tests.

No consensus variant V1--V5 improved on V0. The best candidate (V4, two-channel logistic) gained only +0.0088 LONG-strat, well below the +0.015 selection threshold. V0 stands as the shipped metric.

The rename tradeoff remains the central open problem. V0 has RENAME\_NONCE FA 0.765 on development E and 1.0 on E2: any renaming of predicates breaks the consensus signal. The GG checker was the iteration-5 attempt to solve this. It reduces MEANING\_RENAME endorsement from 0.502 (V0) to 0.224, but fails the development gate (strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742) because the gloss gate rejects too many legitimate predicate mappings (d = 0.629). The name-free consensus line (c\_nf, c\_hyb, GG) has produced no variant that simultaneously achieves low rename FA and high discrimination.

Five limitations bound the current results. First, no confirmatory hypothesis is confirmed or refuted: every confirmation arm was budget-stopped before reaching testability. Second, all evaluation is on FOLIO and MALLS-derived data; domain transfer is untested. Third, the labels are noisy: the panel majority accuracy on expert-curated errors is 0.727, and the R\_COMP FREE audit shows 13--28\% label contamination. Fourth, the consensus advantage does not grow with sentence complexity (M3 INCONCLUSIVE). Fifth, the rename tradeoff is unsolved: no variant achieves both low rename FA and high error recall.

%% ============================================================
\section{Related Work}
%% ============================================================

\textbf{NL-FOL datasets and their quality.} FOLIO~\citep{Han2022} provides 1,435 FOL-annotated NLI problems. MALLS~\citep{Yang2023malls} uses GPT-4 to generate and verify NL-FOL pairs at scale. \citet{Brunello2026} found that approximately 42\% of entries in both datasets contain incorrect FOL formalisations, with additional ambiguity rates of 17.8\% (FOLIO) and 51\% (MALLS). Logic-LM~\citep{Pan2023} prompts LLMs for FOL and calls a prover.

\textbf{FOL closeness metrics.} \citet{Thatikonda2025} evaluate n-gram, graph, embedding, and LLM-based metrics on controlled FOL perturbations, finding that no single metric is sensitive to all perturbation types. Our typed repair operators follow the tradition of \citet{Thatikonda2024} but are derived from z3 equivalence-class differences.

\textbf{Factuality metrics.} FRANK~\citep{Pagnoni2021} defines a typology of factuality errors. QuestEval~\citep{Scialom2021} uses question generation and answering. Our L3 questionnaire layer generates structured questions from the text and checks the formula's answers via z3.

\textbf{Round-trip and self-consistency.} \citet{Amrollahi2026} propose verbalising a formal statement back to natural language and checking consistency. \citet{Li2024} use symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency for Lean/Isabelle autoformalization. Our round-trip baseline achieves only AUROC 0.710 on NL-FOL.

\textbf{Cross-check consistency.} SAC3~\citep{Zhang2023sac3} detects hallucinations via semantic-aware cross-check consistency. Our cross-system consensus metric uses a similar principle with FOL equivalence and multiple model families. The $\Delta$AUROC of cross-family consensus over single-model self-consistency is +0.140.

\textbf{Automated alignment for autoformalization.} FormalAlign trains a model on alignment scoring via a dual contrastive-generative loss. Our approach uses no learned alignment model.

\textbf{Vacuity detection.} \citet{Kupferman2003} formalise vacuity in temporal logic model checking. Our L1 lint layer includes a vacuity check adapted from their framework.

\textbf{Cross-model translation confidence.} \citet{Bayless2025} apply the same score form as c\_score to NL-to-SMT translation. NoTB uses four LLM families for requirements-to-temporal-logic translation.

\textbf{Predicate alignment.} LogicLLaMA~\citep{Yang2023logicllama} uses a greedy binding search. \citet{Vossel2025} map predicates by normalised Levenshtein distance. No prior work reports a rename false-alarm rate.

\textbf{N-version programming.} \citet{Chen1978} noted that ``faulty but identical results may outvote correct results''---precisely the endorsement failure mode we measure (e = 0.124 on E, 0.459 under CSC).

This is expected and fundamental: two formulas with different predicate names are not z3-equivalent, so any rename breaks the equivalence check.\n\n\\subsubsection{Blind-spot analysis}\n\n38\\% of ERROR items are z3-equivalent to the medoid (the most popular peer formula). This places a ceiling on recall of approximately 62\\%. The blind-spot rate is 5\\% for polarity errors and 57\\% for structural errors.\n\n\\subsubsection{Cost}\n\nThe peer pool costs \\$0.0015 per sentence (6 peers via API). It requires peer translations from multiple model families and is fundamentally non-invariant to predicate renaming (96\\% FA under RENAME).\n\\item The disguised cheap judge sets the bar at AUROC 0.777. The S4 combination reaches 0.817 (+0.039, not significant). The frontier judge adds nothing significant over the cheap judge under solver labels; under panel labels the advantage strengthens (+0.166, p $<$ 0.001).\n\\item FOL-Triage achieves AUROC 0.759, below the bar. Its primary value is invariance: the fused flip rate under meaning-preserving rewrites is 0.013, compared to 0.29--0.49 for judges.\n\\item L1 lint does not transfer from human annotation errors to LLM outputs. The pilot structural metrics are null. Round-trip NLI is 0.067 below the judge.\n\\item The evaluation labels are noisy: 58.8\\% of track-L ``errors'' are pure ADD+DROP (likely vocabulary mismatches).\n\\item No contamination was detected for any LLM-based metric.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section{Iteration 2}\n%% ============================================================\n\n\\subsection{Strategy}\n\nIteration 2 has three goals: (i) confirm iteration~1's ordering on the development dataset~E under both the solver labels (R\\_AB, R\\_A) and panel-adjudicated labels (R\\_ADJ); (ii) test whether fusing the consensus signal (PEER) with text-based checks (TEXT = L2-bow + L3) improves over each alone; and (iii) construct a typed perturbation suite (PERTURB) for controlled sensitivity testing.\n\nThe pre-registered bar is the flash-lite judge on disguised sentences, with the local Qwen3-8B judge as fallback. The shared OpenRouter key hit its daily limit before the development-set experiment completed, making the flash-lite bar UNTESTABLE on E.\n\n\\subsection{Experiment 5: PEER+TEXT on development dataset E}\n\nPEER+TEXT is a logistic fusion of the consensus signal (c\\_score\\_align) and the text-based FOL-Triage layers (L2-bow, L3 questionnaire). API spend was \\$0.\n\n\\subsubsection{Headline AUROCs on E (R\\_AB, ERROR vs CORRECT)}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{PEER+TEXT headline AUROCs on development set E.}\n\\label{tab:peertext_e}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lrcccccr}\n\\toprule\nSubset & n (err/cor) & PEER+TEXT & c\\_score\\_align & NF c & L2-bow & L3 & Local judge \\\\\n\\midrule\nR\\_AB pooled & 2686 (1822/864) & 0.790 & 0.782 & 0.743 & 0.734 & 0.579 & 0.712 \\\\\nR\\_AB L25 & 873 (697/176) & 0.755 & 0.712 & 0.651 & 0.722 & 0.560 & 0.664 \\\\\nR\\_AB L20 & 821 (592/229) & 0.747 & 0.722 & 0.643 & 0.715 & 0.547 & 0.683 \\\\\nR\\_AB EXC & 606 (384/222) & 0.777 & 0.814 & 0.782 & 0.669 & 0.620 & 0.663 \\\\\nR\\_AB CTRL & 386 (149/237) & 0.708 & 0.742 & 0.741 & 0.613 & 0.490 & 0.739 \\\\\nR\\_AB long pool & 2300 (1673/627) & 0.768 & 0.759 & 0.704 & 0.717 & 0.580 & 0.653 \\\\\nR\\_A L20+EXC & 449 (261/188) & 0.818 & 0.860 & 0.802 & 0.678 & 0.587 & 0.554 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_dev_set_auroc_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{AUROCs on development set E by metric and subset. PEER+TEXT leads on R\\_AB pooled (0.790); the local judge lags at 0.712.}\n  \\label{fig:dev_set_auroc}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe paired $\\Delta$AUROC of PEER+TEXT minus the local judge is +0.078 [0.043, 0.112] on R\\_AB pooled (DeLong p $<$ 0.0001). On the long pool, the gap widens to +0.115 [0.075, 0.157].\n\nThe stratified AUROC (pairing only within complexity strata) shows PEER+TEXT at 0.753 and c\\_score\\_align at 0.741, a difference of +0.011 [$-$0.012, 0.038], not significant. The TEXT layers add no significant discriminative power over c\\_score\\_align alone once the stratum-composition confound is removed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Mechanism predictions}\n\n\\textbf{P1 (PEER catches COVERAGE errors that TEXT misses, and vice versa).} At matched false-alarm rate 0.10: PEER has higher recall than TEXT on COVERAGE errors (+0.093 [0.046, 0.147]), and TEXT has higher recall on PEER\\_ENDORSED errors (+0.103 [0.051, 0.171]). Verdict: INCONCLUSIVE.\n\n\\textbf{P2 (PEER and TEXT error rankings are uncorrelated).} Spearman correlation between PEER and TEXT among errors is 0.294 [0.224, 0.365]. Verdict: REFUTED.\n\n\\textbf{P3 (PEER+TEXT advantage grows with sentence complexity).} The logistic interaction term is $-$0.023 [$-$0.228, 0.185], consistent with no interaction. Verdict: INCONCLUSIVE.\n\n\\textbf{P4 (PEER+TEXT is more invariant to meaning-preserving rewrites than judges).} RENAME FA: fused 0.385, local judge 0.683. Key corrections: E is development data (not held-out); T2 NOT CONFIRMED; MEANING\\_RENAME is an ERROR operator; cost units corrected.\n\n\\subsection{Iteration 5 Summary}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_confirmation_landscape_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Confirmation landscape across all five iterations. Every confirmation arm was budget-stopped before reaching testability. The DT stratum (V0 0.916) is the only testable cell.}\n  \\label{fig:confirmation_landscape}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item \\textbf{Confirmation is NOT\\_TESTABLE across the board.} The run-wide budget (\\$7.00) was exhausted before any confirmation arm could complete.\n\\item \\textbf{DT stratum is a bright spot.} V0 reaches strat AUROC 0.916 [0.858, 0.970] on 179 ProverQA-derived rows with trusted gold.\n\\item \\textbf{L25 on E2 is near chance.} V0 strat AUROC 0.443 on E2-A L25 (42 rows).\n\\item \\textbf{R\\_COMP FREE provisional results favour consensus.} c\\_align 0.801 vs judge 0.584 ($\\Delta$ +0.217 [+0.175, +0.260]).\n\\item \\textbf{V0 stands.} No variant V1--V5 met the selection rule.\n\\item \\textbf{GG fails its development gate.} Strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742.\n\\item \\textbf{Rename weakness persists.} V0 RENAME\\_NONCE FA 1.0 on E2.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Dead ends accumulated across all iterations.}\n\\label{tab:dead_ends_final}\n\\begin{tabular}{llp{6cm}}\n\\toprule\nDead end & Iter & Reason \\\\\n\\midrule\nL1 lint on LLM outputs & 1 & AUROC 0.508 \\\\\nL2 role-aware & 1 & AUROC 0.557 \\\\\nPilot structural metrics & 1 & AUROC 0.500--0.533 \\\\\nRound-trip reformalisation & 1 & AUROC 0.513 (76\\% ties) \\\\\nB2 decomposed z3 reader & 2 & Gate balanced accuracy 0.476 \\\\\nR\\_ADJ LLM adjudicator & 2 & Sonnet-5 balanced accuracy 0.662 \\\\\nName-free consensus (c\\_nf) & 2--3 & SWAP recall 0.512 \\\\\nCSC & 4 & Provisional: strat AUROC 0.614, e = 0.459 \\\\\nGG (Gloss-Gated) & 5 & Gate g3 FAIL: strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section{What We Have Learned So Far}\n%% ============================================================\n\nThe cross-family consensus metric (c\\_score\\_align) is the strongest gold-free faithfulness signal found in this investigation. On development set E, it achieves stratified AUROC 0.742, beating the best cheap LLM judge (0.641) by +0.101 [+0.053, +0.145]. On R\\_COMP SIG (the out-of-scope controlled-vocabulary condition), it reaches 0.954 within-template AUROC with zero error endorsement. Three peer families suffice for 97\\% of full-pool performance (M4 confirmed: k95 = 3; by words tercile k95 = 2/3/5).\n\nThe mechanism is clear: errors scatter across z3-equivalence classes while correct translations cluster. The consensus signal degrades with sentence length (NET +0.401 on development E, driven by divergence d), meaning longer sentences need more peers and the metric becomes less reliable precisely where it matters most.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_vocabulary_source_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{The vocabulary source problem. c\\_align RENAME\\_NONCE FA is 0.765 on development E and 1.0 on E2: any renaming of predicates breaks the consensus signal. The GG checker reduces MEANING\\_RENAME endorsement from 0.502 (V0) to 0.224 but fails the development gate (strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742) because the gloss gate rejects too many legitimate predicate mappings.}\n  \\label{fig:vocabulary_source}\n\\end{figure}\n\nIteration 5 attempted confirmation on three fronts, and all three were blocked by the run-wide budget (\\$7.00). E2-A produced one testable cell: V0 reaches 0.916 on ProverQA-derived sentences with trusted gold, but only 0.443 on the L25 long-sentence stratum (near chance). E2-B's exploratory results (V0 0.737 vs flash-lite 0.496, $\\Delta$ +0.208) favour consensus on long sentences with unaudited labels, but the label-coupling diagnostic shows part of the advantage comes from shared gold-equivalent peers. R\\_COMP FREE's provisional results show c\\_align 0.801 vs judge 0.584 ($\\Delta$ +0.217) under ERROR\\_CERT vs MAPPED labels, with consensus carrying most of the signal in nesting tests.\n\nNo consensus variant V1--V5 improved on V0. The best candidate (V4, two-channel logistic) gained only +0.0088 LONG-strat, well below the +0.015 selection threshold. V0 stands as the shipped metric.\n\nThe rename tradeoff remains the central open problem. V0 has RENAME\\_NONCE FA 0.765 on development E and 1.0 on E2: any renaming of predicates breaks the consensus signal. The GG checker was the iteration-5 attempt to solve this. It reduces MEANING\\_RENAME endorsement from 0.502 (V0) to 0.224, but fails the development gate (strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742) because the gloss gate rejects too many legitimate predicate mappings (d = 0.629). The name-free consensus line (c\\_nf, c\\_hyb, GG) has produced no variant that simultaneously achieves low rename FA and high discrimination.\n\nFive limitations bound the current results. First, no confirmatory hypothesis is confirmed or refuted: every confirmation arm was budget-stopped before reaching testability. Second, all evaluation is on FOLIO and MALLS-derived data; domain transfer is untested. Third, the labels are noisy: the panel majority accuracy on expert-curated errors is 0.727, and the R\\_COMP FREE audit shows 13--28\\% label contamination. Fourth, the consensus advantage does not grow with sentence complexity (M3 INCONCLUSIVE). Fifth, the rename tradeoff is unsolved: no variant achieves both low rename FA and high error recall.\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section{Related Work}\n%% ============================================================\n\n\\textbf{NL-FOL datasets and their quality.} FOLIO~\\citep{Han2022} provides 1,435 FOL-annotated NLI problems. MALLS~\\citep{Yang2023malls} uses GPT-4 to generate and verify NL-FOL pairs at scale. \\citet{Brunello2026} found that approximately 42\\% of entries in both datasets contain incorrect FOL formalisations, with additional ambiguity rates of 17.8\\% (FOLIO) and 51\\% (MALLS). Logic-LM~\\citep{Pan2023} prompts LLMs for FOL and calls a prover.\n\n\\textbf{FOL closeness metrics.} \\citet{Thatikonda2025} evaluate n-gram, graph, embedding, and LLM-based metrics on controlled FOL perturbations, finding that no single metric is sensitive to all perturbation types. Our typed repair operators follow the tradition of \\citet{Thatikonda2024} but are derived from z3 equivalence-class differences.\n\n\\textbf{Factuality metrics.} FRANK~\\citep{Pagnoni2021} defines a typology of factuality errors. QuestEval~\\citep{Scialom2021} uses question generation and answering. Our L3 questionnaire layer generates structured questions from the text and checks the formula's answers via z3.\n\n\\textbf{Round-trip and self-consistency.} \\citet{Amrollahi2026} propose verbalising a formal statement back to natural language and checking consistency. \\citet{Li2024} use symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency for Lean/Isabelle autoformalization. Our round-trip baseline achieves only AUROC 0.710 on NL-FOL.\n\n\\textbf{Cross-check consistency.} SAC3~\\citep{Zhang2023sac3} detects hallucinations via semantic-aware cross-check consistency. Our cross-system consensus metric uses a similar principle with FOL equivalence and multiple model families. The $\\Delta$AUROC of cross-family consensus over single-model self-consistency is +0.140.\n\n\\textbf{Automated alignment for autoformalization.} FormalAlign trains a model on alignment scoring via a dual contrastive-generative loss. Our approach uses no learned alignment model.\n\n\\textbf{Vacuity detection.} \\citet{Kupferman2003} formalise vacuity in temporal logic model checking. Our L1 lint layer includes a vacuity check adapted from their framework.\n\n\\textbf{Cross-model translation confidence.} \\citet{Bayless2025} apply the same score form as c\\_score to NL-to-SMT translation. \documentclass[11pt,letterpaper]{article}
\usepackage{graphicx, geometry, amsmath, hyperref, url, booktabs, xcolor}
\geometry{margin=1in}
\hypersetup{colorlinks=true, linkcolor=black, citecolor=black, urlcolor=black}
\usepackage{enumitem}

\title{Gold-Free Faithfulness Metrics for NL-to-FOL Translation\\[0.5em]\large Executive Summary}
\author{Internal Research Report}
\date{September 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Problem}

Translating natural language into first-order logic (NL-FOL) is a prerequisite for neurosymbolic reasoning, yet evaluating whether a candidate formula faithfully captures a sentence's meaning remains an open problem. Gold FOL annotations are expensive, non-unique, and unreliable: approximately 42\% of entries in both FOLIO and MALLS contain incorrect formalisations. This investigation seeks gold-free metrics that predict faithfulness given only a sentence and a candidate formula, with no reference formula, no ontology, and no domain knowledge.

\section{Approach}

Over five iterations, we screened four metric families on a frozen evaluation set and a 700-sentence development set (E):

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{FOL-Triage}: a three-layer cascade (L1 formula lint, L2 bag-of-words text accounting, L3 role questionnaire with z3 formula reading).
\item \textbf{Round-trip verification}: verbalise the formula back to natural language and compare via NLI.
\item \textbf{Cross-system consensus}: collect independent translations from multiple LLM families, score by z3-equivalence agreement with the peer pool.
\item \textbf{LLM judges}: direct scoring by cheap and frontier LLMs, with nonce disguise to control for memorisation.
\end{itemize}

The evaluation is a meta-evaluation: we build labelled (sentence, formula) pairs from audited public benchmarks and measure each metric's AUROC for discriminating correct translations from errors. All confidence intervals are sentence-clustered percentile bootstrap (B = 2000, seed 0).

\section{Key Findings}

\subsection{Cross-family consensus is the strongest signal}

The cross-family consensus metric (c\_score\_align) achieves stratified AUROC 0.742 on development set E, beating the best cheap LLM judge (flash-lite disguised, 0.641) by +0.101 [+0.053, +0.145]. Three peer families suffice for 97\% of full-pool performance.

On R\_COMP SIG (controlled-vocabulary composed sentences, 221 sentences), consensus reaches within-template AUROC 0.954 with zero error endorsement, vs the judge's 0.587 ($\Delta$ = +0.367).

Adding c\_score\_align to a 28-feature baseline stack (S4\_full) yields +0.039 [+0.021, +0.057] stratified AUROC. A 4-feature model (c\_score\_align, L2-bow, L3, p\_text) matches the full stack without any judge features.

\subsection{The rename tradeoff is unsolved}

The consensus metric depends on shared predicate vocabulary between the candidate and its peers. Renaming predicates breaks the z3 equivalence check:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Variant & RENAME\_NONCE FA & SWAP recall \\
\midrule
c\_align (shipped V0) & 0.765 & 0.758 \\
c\_nf (name-free) & 0.132 & 0.512 \\
c\_hyb (hybrid) & 0.216 & 0.832 \\
GG (Gloss-Gated) & gate FAIL & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

No consensus variant achieves both low rename false-alarm rate and high structural-error recall. The GG checker (iteration 5) reduced MEANING\_RENAME endorsement from 0.502 to 0.224 but failed the development gate (strat AUROC 0.696 vs V0 0.742).

\subsection{Confirmation was blocked by budget}

All three confirmation arms (E2-A: 110 sentences, E2-B: 400 long sentences, R\_COMP FREE) were budget-stopped before reaching testability. The one testable cell---DT stratum on E2-A (179 ProverQA-derived rows with trusted gold)---yields V0 strat AUROC 0.916 [0.858, 0.970]. The L25 long-sentence stratum shows V0 near chance (0.443, 42 rows).

\subsection{Dead ends}

Nine approaches were tried and dropped:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
Dead end & Iter & Key number \\
\midrule
L1 lint on LLM outputs & 1 & AUROC 0.508 \\
L2 role-aware & 1 & AUROC 0.557 \\
Pilot structural metrics & 1 & AUROC 0.500--0.533 \\
Round-trip reformalisation & 1 & AUROC 0.513 \\
B2 decomposed z3 reader & 2 & Gate BA 0.476 \\
R\_ADJ LLM adjudicator & 2 & Sonnet-5 BA 0.662 \\
Name-free consensus (c\_nf) & 2--3 & SWAP recall 0.512 \\
CSC (Candidate-Signature) & 4 & Strat AUROC 0.614 \\
GG (Gloss-Gated) & 5 & Strat AUROC 0.696 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{Limitations}

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \textbf{No confirmation.} Every confirmation arm was budget-stopped before reaching testability.
\item \textbf{Domain scope.} All evaluation is on FOLIO and MALLS-derived data; domain transfer is untested.
\item \textbf{Label noise.} Panel majority accuracy on expert-curated errors is 0.727; R\_COMP FREE audit shows 13--28\% label contamination.
\item \textbf{No complexity scaling.} The consensus advantage does not grow with sentence complexity (M3 INCONCLUSIVE).
\item \textbf{Rename tradeoff unsolved.} No variant achieves both low rename FA and high error recall.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Shipped Metric}

V0 (c\_score\_align) stands as the shipped metric. No variant V1--V5 met the pre-registered selection rule (the best candidate, V4, gained only +0.0088 LONG-strat, below the +0.015 threshold).

\textbf{Cost:} \$0.000121 per item (consensus) vs \$0.0000488 per item (flash-lite judge). At k = 3 peer families: \$0.000946 per sentence.

\textbf{Operating envelope:} strongest on exception-clause sentences (AUROC 0.964 on ``except'' sentences) and on sentences with 12+ words where judges degrade. Weakest on short simple sentences (CTRL: consensus $-$0.069 vs judge, n.s.) and on vocabulary-mismatch errors (MEANING\_RENAME recall 0.07 at FA 0.10).

\section{Total API Spend}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
Iteration & Spend \\
\midrule
1 (screen) & \$13.66 \\
2 (dev set E + PERTURB) & \$4.23 \\
3 (API bar + R\_COMP + PERTURB) & \$4.33 \\
4 (CSC + E2 + FREE labels) & \$0.35 \\
5 (E2-A/B + R\_COMP FREE + freeze) & \$4.02 \\
\midrule
\textbf{Total} & \textbf{\$26.59} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\end{document}

MALLS~\\citep{Yang2023malls} uses GPT-4 to generate and verify NL-FOL pairs at scale. \\citet{Brunello2026} found that approximately 42\\% of entries in both datasets contain incorrect FOL formalisations, with additional ambiguity rates of 17.8\\% (FOLIO) and 51\\% (MALLS). Logic-LM~\\citep{Pan2023} prompts LLMs for FOL and calls a prover.\n\n\\textbf{FOL closeness metrics.} \\citet{Thatikonda2025} evaluate n-gram, graph, embedding, and LLM-based metrics on controlled FOL perturbations, finding that no single metric is sensitive to all perturbation types. Our typed repair operators follow the tradition of \\citet{Thatikonda2024} but are derived from z3 equivalence-class differences.\n\n\\textbf{Factuality metrics.} FRANK~\\citep{Pagnoni2021} defines a typology of factuality errors. QuestEval~\\citep{Scialom2021} uses question generation and answering. Our L3 questionnaire layer generates structured questions from the text and checks the formula's answers via z3.\n\n\\textbf{Round-trip and self-consistency.} \\citet{Amrollahi2026} propose verbalising a formal statement back to natural language and checking consistency. \\citet{Li2024} use symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency for Lean/Isabelle autoformalization. Our round-trip baseline achieves only AUROC 0.710 on NL-FOL.\n\n\\textbf{Cross-check consistency.} SAC3~\\citep{Zhang2023sac3} detects hallucinations via semantic-aware cross-check consistency. Our cross-system consensus metric uses a similar principle with FOL equivalence and multiple model families. The $\\Delta$AUROC of cross-family consensus over single-model self-consistency is +0.140.\n\n\\textbf{Automated alignment for autoformalization.} FormalAlign trains a model on alignment scoring via a dual contrastive-generative loss. Our approach uses no learned alignment model.\n\n\\textbf{Vacuity detection.} \\citet{Kupferman2003} formalise vacuity in temporal logic model checking. Our L1 lint layer includes a vacuity check adapted from their framework.\n\n\\textbf{Cross-model translation confidence.} \\citet{Bayless2025} apply the same score form as c\\_score to NL-to-SMT translation. NoTB uses four LLM families for requirements-to-temporal-logic translation.\n\n\\textbf{Predicate alignment.} LogicLLaMA~\\citep{Yang2023logicllama} uses a greedy binding search. \\citet{Vossel2025} map predicates by normalised Levenshtein distance. No prior work reports a rename false-alarm rate.\n\n\\textbf{N-version programming.} \\citet{Chen1978} noted that ``faulty but identical results may outvote correct results''---precisely the endorsement failure mode we measure (e = 0.124 on E, 0.459 under CSC).\n\n%% ============================================================\n\\section*{References}\n%% ============================================================\n\n\\begin{thebibliography}{26}\n\n\\bibitem[Han et~al.(2022)]{Han2022}\nSimeng Han, Hailey Schoelkopf, Yilun Zhao, et~al.\n\\newblock FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic.\n\\newblock In \\emph{EMNLP}, 2022.\n\n\\bibitem[Yang et~al.(2023a)]{Yang2023malls}\nDelong Yang, Fei Huang, and Yongbin Li.\n\\newblock MALLS: A Multi-task Benchmark for Automated Logical Specification.\n\\newblock \\emph{ArXiv}, abs/2305.18100, 2023.\n\n\\bibitem[Brunello et~al.(2026)]{Brunello2026}\nAndrea Brunello, Cristian Curaba, Luca Geatti, Michele Mignani, Angelo Montanari, and N.~Saccomanno.\n\\newblock Fixing FOLIO and MALLS: Verified Annotations and an LLM-assisted Framework to Focus Human Relabeling.\n\\newblock \\emph{ArXiv}, abs/2606.02837, 2026.\n\n\\bibitem[Brunello et~al.(2025)]{Brunello2025}\nAndrea Brunello, Luca Geatti, Michele Mignani, Angelo Montanari, and N.~Saccomanno.\n\\newblock Do LLMs Really Struggle at NL-FOL Translation?\n\\newblock In \\emph{AAAI}, 2025.\n\n\\bibitem[Thatikonda et~al.(2025)]{Thatikonda2025}\nRamya~K. File: /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_An1uy2kF2SjZ/4_gen_paper_repo/_4_assemble_paper/report_workspace/README.md

# Gold-Free Faithfulness Metrics for NL-to-FOL Translation

Internal research report assembled from 5 iterations of investigation into cross-family solver consensus as a gold-free metric for evaluating NL-to-FOL translation faithfulness. The report covers 22 artifact workspaces (14 experiments, 4 evaluations, 3 datasets, 1 research study), typesets 50+ result tables, and includes 8 data figures.

## Layout

| Path | Description |
|---|---|
| `report.tex` | Full LaTeX source (36 pages, all 22 artifacts referenced by name) |
| `report.pdf` | Compiled report |
| `exec_summary.tex` | Executive summary LaTeX source (3 pages) |
| `exec_summary.pdf` | Compiled executive summary |
| `references.bib` | BibTeX bibliography (22 entries; not used by bibtex, kept as source) |
| `figures/` | 8 pre-generated vector PDF figures |
| `.aii/manifest.yaml` | Artifact manifest with keep/delete decisions |
| `.terminal_claude_agent_struct_out.json` | Structured output for the assembly pipeline |

## Compilation

No bibtex step is needed — the bibliography is inline via `thebibliography`.

```bash
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode report.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode report.tex
```

For the executive summary:

```bash
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode exec_summary.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode exec_summary.tex
```

## Restoring removed files

LaTeX auxiliary files (`.aux`, `.log`, `.out`, `.toc`) are marked as deletable. To restore them, recompile:

```bash
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode report.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode report.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode exec_summary.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode exec_summary.tex
```
