--- Item 1 ---
id: fig_rewrite_fa
figure_type: data
title: Rewrite False-Alarm Rates
caption: >-
  False-alarm (FA) rate of FOL-Triage layers and the fused score under five families of meaning-preserving rewrites, measured
  on track-L CORRECT items (each family applies to only the $n$ of 150 items shown under its name). Bars give the fraction
  of rewritten CORRECT items flagged by L1 lint (grey), L2 bag-of-words (blue), L2 role-aware (green), L3 questionnaire (orange)
  and the fused score (red); error bars are Wilson 95\% confidence intervals. White diamonds mark the fused score's FA on
  the same items \emph{before} rewriting, and the dashed line is the pre-registered 10\% gate. PRENEX applies to a single
  item, where every layer's FA is 0 (CI not drawn). L1, L2 role-aware and L3 stay below the gate for every family, and L2
  bag-of-words exceeds it only under RENAME (0.18). The fused score (0.18--0.275) is above the gate for every family with
  $n>1$, but its FA on the original formulas is the same or higher (0.23--0.275), and its verdict flips on at most 6.1\% of
  items. So the fused false alarms come from its calibration being fitted on track H, not from the rewrites.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Grouped bar chart. X-axis: five rewrite families (RENAME, REORDER, DEMORGAN, CONTRAPOSITIVE, PRENEX). Y-axis: false-alarm
  rate (0.0 to 0.30). Six bars per group, one per metric layer. Values — RENAME: L1=0.0, L2-bow=0.18, L2-role=0.013, L3=0.033,
  Fused=0.22, Cascade=0.22. REORDER: L1=0.0, bow=0.029, role=0.059, L3=0.059, Fused=0.235, Cascade=0.235. DEMORGAN: L1=0.0,
  bow=0.030, role=0.061, L3=0.030, Fused=0.182, Cascade=0.182. CONTRAPOSITIVE: L1=0.025, bow=0.10, role=0.025, L3=0.025, Fused=0.275,
  Cascade=0.275. PRENEX: all 0.0. Colors: L1 light grey, L2-bow blue, L2-role teal, L3 orange, Fused red, Cascade dark red.
  Dashed horizontal line at y=0.10 labelled '10% gate'. White background, sans-serif font, legend at top right.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  FOL-Triage's individual layers pass the 10% rewrite FA gate; only the fused score fails due to calibration mismatch.
figure_path: figures/fig_rewrite_fa_v0.pdf

--- Item 2 ---
id: fig_consensus_auroc
figure_type: data
title: Consensus Metric AUROCs
caption: >-
  AUROC for detecting unfaithful formulas on the iteration-1 development screen (track L: Logic-LM outputs on FOLIO validation
  labelled by Z3 equivalence to corrected gold; $n=546$, 249 errors, 297 correct). Bars start at chance (0.5); error bars
  are sentence-clustered bootstrap 95\% CIs. Blue bars are cross-family consensus (c\_score) variants, orange bars are metrics
  computed from self-consistency (SC) samples, and grey bars are other metrics. SC-5 same model is defined only for the $n=167$
  GPT-3.5 candidates, and Misalignment uses the gold reference, so it is a confound probe rather than a gold-free metric.
  The dashed line marks the disguised cheap LLM judge (AUROC 0.777), scored in a companion experiment on an overlapping track-L
  set of $n=524$. The three consensus variants that draw on multiple model families rank highest (0.863--0.872), above every
  self-consistency baseline (at most 0.725) and the judge line. Restricting peers to the two other Logic-LM systems drops
  c\_score to 0.753.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Horizontal bar chart. Y-axis labels (top to bottom): c_score (all peers), c_score (6 fresh), c_score (non-OpenAI), Misalignment,
  cluster entropy, Pred-set instability (pool), c_score (2 Logic-LM), SC-5 cheap, SC-5 same model, medoid depth, Pred-set
  instability (SC), SC-5 entropy, FOL length. X-axis: AUROC from 0.4 to 1.0. Values: 0.866, 0.872, 0.863, 0.835, 0.773, 0.770,
  0.753, 0.725, 0.716, 0.722, 0.688, 0.631, 0.527. Error bars showing 95% CI. Bars colored blue for consensus variants, orange
  for SC variants, grey for others. Vertical dashed line at 0.777 labelled 'cheap judge bar'. White background, sans-serif
  font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: Cross-family consensus dominates all other metrics and baselines in iteration 1.
figure_path: figures/fig_consensus_auroc_v0.pdf

id: fig_baseline_auroc
figure_type: data
title: Baseline AUROCs on Screen
caption: >-
  AUROC of all 28 baseline metrics and judge variants for separating erroneous from correct formalisations on the iteration-1
  screen (track L, $n=524$: 230 erroneous, 294 correct), sorted from highest to lowest. Each bar starts at chance (solid line,
  0.5), so its length is the AUROC gained over chance. Whiskers are 95\% sentence-clustered bootstrap CIs (2{,}000 resamples),
  and the number beside each row is the point estimate. Green bars are LLM judges, blue bars are round-trip (FOL$\to$NL$\to$compare)
  metrics and grey bars are structural checks (the pilot metrics and parse failure). Hatched bars were scored only on the
  pre-registered 200-item subset (68 erroneous, 132 correct), and pilot\_rerun\_jacc covers 505 items. The dashed line marks
  the bar of 0.777 [0.720, 0.827] set by the disguised flash-lite judge (judge\_cheap\_disg), the highest baseline on the
  full set. Only the frontier judge on original text (judge\_strong\_orig, 0.802 [0.715, 0.877], subset) is higher. Its CI
  overlaps the bar, and on disguised text it falls to 0.730. The static structural checks and parse failure sit at chance
  (0.500--0.533, with every CI covering 0.5). Only the rerun-stability metric pilot\_rerun\_jacc carries signal (0.720).
image_gen_detailed_description: >-

--- Item 4 ---
id: fig_summary_comparison
figure_type: data
title: Iteration 1 Summary Comparison
caption: >-
  Discrimination versus rename invariance for the metric families screened in iteration 1. The $x$-axis is the flip rate under
  the meaning-preserving RENAME rewrite: the fraction of track-L CORRECT items ($n=150$; 149 scored for consensus) whose binary
  verdict changes after renaming. Error bars are Wilson 95\% intervals. The $y$-axis is item-level AUROC for separating ERROR
  from CORRECT candidates, with the 95\% CI reported by each experiment ($n=546$ for c\_score, 524 for the judge and round-trip,
  477 for FOL-Triage and L1 lint). Each point is labelled with its per-item cost (per sentence for consensus). Points: c\_score
  consensus (red diamond), disguised cheap LLM judge judge\_cheap\_disg (orange square), FOL-Triage fused (green circle),
  round-trip rt\_nli\_min (purple triangle), and L1 lint (grey inverted triangle). The grey dashed line marks the bar, the
  judge's AUROC of 0.777. The blue dotted line marks the cross-fitted S4 combination of all cheap features (AUROC 0.817 [0.762,
  0.867]); no rewrite flip rate was measured for it, so it is drawn as a line rather than a point. Consensus has the highest
  AUROC (0.866) but flips on 77\% of renamed items (its RENAME false-alarm rate is 96\%). FOL-Triage is nearly rename-invariant
  (flip rate 0.013) but falls below the bar (0.759). No metric sits in the high-AUROC, low-flip corner.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Scatter plot. X-axis: RENAME rewrite flip rate (0.0 to 1.0). Y-axis: AUROC (0.4 to 0.95). Points with labels: c_score (0.96,
  0.866), S4 combo (0.39, 0.817), judge_cheap_disg (0.39, 0.777), FOL-Triage fused (0.013, 0.759), rt_nli_min (0.31, 0.710),
  L1 lint (0.0, 0.508). Point sizes proportional to cost. Colors: consensus red, baselines blue, judge orange, FOL-Triage
  green, round-trip purple, L1 grey. Horizontal dashed line at 0.777 labelled 'bar'. White background, sans-serif font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  Trade-off between discriminative power (AUROC) and invariance (flip rate) across metric families.
figure_path: figures/fig_summary_comparison_v0.pdf

--- Item 5 ---
id: fig_dev_set_auroc
figure_type: data
title: Development Set E AUROCs
caption: >-
  Item-level AUROC for separating ERROR from CORRECT candidates on development dataset E. Each group is one subset: the R\_AB
  population (label tiers A+B) pooled (n = 2,686 items; 1,822 ERROR, 864 CORRECT, 292 sentences), its L25, L20, exception
  (EXC) and control (CTRL) strata, the long pool (L25+L20+EXC), and the tier-A-only R\_A L20+EXC subset. The R\_A subset sits
  to the right of the dotted line, and n below each group counts its scored items. Bars are PEER+TEXT (vermillion), c\_score\_align
  (blue), NF c\_score (green), L2-bow (orange), L3 (reddish purple) and the disguised local Qwen3-8B judge (grey). Bars start
  at the dashed chance line (AUROC = 0.5), and whiskers are 95\% sentence-cluster bootstrap CIs. The two consensus-based scores
  lead on every subset. PEER+TEXT is highest on R\_AB pooled (0.790), L25, L20 and the long pool (0.768). c\_score\_align
  is highest on EXC (0.814), CTRL and R\_A L20+EXC (0.860), and on every subset its interval overlaps PEER+TEXT's. Both consensus
  scores sit above the local judge on every subset except CTRL. The gap is widest on the long, exception-clause R\_A L20+EXC
  subset, where the judge falls to 0.554. L3 is the weakest score on every subset except R\_A L20+EXC, ranging from 0.490
  to 0.620. No metric separates clearly from the others on CTRL, where the intervals are widest.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Grouped bar chart. X-axis: seven data subsets (R_AB pooled, R_AB L25, R_AB L20, R_AB EXC, R_AB CTRL, R_AB long pool, R_A
  L20+EXC). Y-axis: AUROC (0.4 to 0.95). Six bars per group for metrics: PEER+TEXT, c_score_align, NF c_score, L2-bow, L3,
  Local judge. Values for R_AB pooled: 0.790, 0.782, 0.743, 0.734, 0.579, 0.712. Values for R_A L20+EXC: 0.818, 0.860, 0.802,
  0.678, 0.587, 0.554. Error bars showing 95% CI. Colors: PEER+TEXT red, c_score blue, NF green, L2-bow orange, L3 purple,
  judge grey. White background, sans-serif font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  PEER+TEXT leads on development set E; consensus advantage is largest on long, complex, exception-clause sentences.
figure_path: figures/fig_dev_set_auroc_v0.pdf

--- Item 6 ---
id: fig_csc_anchoring
figure_type: data
title: CSC Anchoring Effect
caption: >-
  Candidate-Signature Consensus (CSC, vermilion) versus free consensus (FREE\_exact, blue) on development set E (354 rows:
  196 ERROR, 158 CORRECT; 144 sentences). (a) Error endorsement $e$, the rate at which peers endorse an erroneous candidate
  (ERROR rows): CSC raises it from 0.173 to 0.459 (arrow, $+0.286$, anchoring). (b) Correct-row divergence $d$ (CORRECT rows):
  CSC lowers it from 0.323 to 0.139 (arrow, $-0.184$, convergence). Lower is better in both (a) and (b), which show point
  estimates; the source reports no interval for $e$ or $d$. (c) Stratified AUROC for separating ERROR from CORRECT rows, with
  95\% CIs (bars) and chance at 0.5 (dashed): CSC 0.614 [0.493, 0.736] lies below FREE\_exact 0.770 [0.686, 0.844], c\_score\_align
  0.774 [0.682, 0.857] and p\_peer\_text 0.799 [0.700, 0.880] (grey). Giving peers the candidate's own symbols buys convergence
  on correct rows at the price of anchoring on errors, a net loss in discriminative power. This is a provisional negative
  on a completion-selected subset of E.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Side-by-side grouped bar chart with two panels. Left panel title: 'Error Endorsement (e)'. Right panel title: 'Correct-Row
  Divergence (d)'. Each panel has two bars: CSC (red) and FREE_exact (blue). Left panel values: CSC e=0.459, FREE e=0.173.
  Right panel values: CSC d=0.139, FREE d=0.323. Y-axis 0.0 to 0.5. Annotation arrow on left panel pointing from FREE bar
  to CSC bar labelled '+0.286 (anchoring)'. Annotation arrow on right panel pointing from FREE bar to CSC bar labelled '-0.184
  (convergence)'. Below both panels, a third mini-panel showing strat AUROC: CSC 0.614, FREE 0.770, c_score_align 0.774, p_peer_text
  0.799. White background, sans-serif font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  CSC raises error endorsement from 0.173 to 0.459 through anchoring while lowering divergence from 0.323 to 0.139. The net
  effect is negative: strat AUROC drops from 0.770 (FREE) to 0.614 (CSC).
figure_path: figures/fig_csc_anchoring_v0.pdf

--- Item 7 ---
id: fig_vocabulary_source
figure_type: data
title: Vocabulary Source Problem
caption: >-
  The vocabulary-source tradeoff for cross-family consensus. For each of four regimes, bars show error endorsement $e$ (blue;
  fraction of ERROR candidates endorsed by the peer majority, lower is better), correct-row divergence $d$ (amber; fraction
  of CORRECT candidates the peers disagree with, lower is better) and AUROC (green; whiskers are 95\% CIs). Tick labels give
  the regime and the data it was measured on, and grey badges give each regime's verdict. External vocabulary (SIG) reaches
  AUROC 0.954 with $e=0$, but it was measured on R\_COMP with a controlled, shared vocabulary, which is out of scope ($\dagger$:
  within-template AUROC; no CI reported). Candidate vocabulary (CSC) lowers $d$ to 0.139 but anchors peers into the candidate's
  errors ($e=0.459$), giving AUROC 0.614. This is a provisional negative on a 354-row completion-selected subset of development
  set E. Independent vocabulary (FREE, exact matching on the same 354 rows) keeps $e$ at 0.173 at the cost of $d=0.323$ (AUROC
  0.770). Gloss-gated filtering (GG, iteration 5, 2{,}672 rows of E) cuts $e$ to 0.081 but raises $d$ to 0.629 (AUROC 0.696)
  and fails its development gate g3. The CSC, FREE and GG AUROCs are stratified AUROCs on development set E, so SIG is not
  directly comparable with the other three.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Conceptual diagram with four columns. Column headers: 'SIG (external vocab)', 'CSC (candidate vocab)', 'FREE (independent
  vocab)', 'GG (gloss-gated)'. Each column shows a flow: Sentence at top, arrow down to 'Peers translate using [source] vocabulary',
  arrow down to metric box. SIG column: e=0.0, d=0.260, AUROC=0.954. CSC column: e=0.459, d=0.139, AUROC=0.614. FREE column:
  e=0.173, d=0.323 (E); d_floor=0.402 (R_COMP). GG column: e=0.081, d=0.629, AUROC=0.696. Below each column a verdict badge:
  SIG='Best but requires ontology (out of scope)', CSC='Provisional negative (anchoring)', FREE='V0 shipped; rename unsolved',
  GG='Gate g3 FAIL (d too high)'. Colors: SIG column green-tinted, CSC column red-tinted, FREE column yellow-tinted, GG column
  orange-tinted. Arrows from candidate formula to CSC peers are red (indicating contamination path). White background, clean
  diagram style, sans-serif font.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  The four vocabulary regimes for consensus and their fundamental tradeoffs. External vocabulary is ideal but requires an
  ontology; candidate vocabulary introduces anchoring; independent vocabulary raises divergence; gloss-gated filtering reduces
  e but raises d further.
figure_path: figures/fig_vocabulary_source_v0.pdf

--- Item 8 ---
id: fig_confirmation_landscape
figure_type: data
title: Confirmation Landscape
caption: >-
  Iteration-5 confirmation attempts and their outcomes. Rows are the three pre-registered confirmation arms: E2-A (110 of
  550 sentences panel-labelled), E2-B (400 sentences) and R_COMP FREE (2,265 parseable rows). Columns give the testability
  status, the stratified AUROC for predicting ERROR with its 95\% CI and $n$ for cross-family consensus (V0, \texttt{c\_score\_align})
  and for the LLM judge, and the pre-registered verdict. Cell colour encodes status: blue = testable cell, pale yellow = exploratory/provisional
  (non-confirmatory), vermillion = not testable. The only testable cells are E2-A's prover-built DT stratum, where V0 reaches
  0.916 [0.858, 0.970] and the local Qwen3-8B judge, substituted for the missing flash-lite bar, reaches 0.913 [0.858, 0.958]
  ($n=179$). This stratum is not the target. On the target long pool (L25+EXC: 18 CORRECT rows), V0 reaches 0.443 on L25 ($n=42$).
  In E2-B and R_COMP FREE, V0 scores above the flash-lite judge (0.737 vs.\ 0.496; 0.801 vs.\ 0.584), but only as exploratory
  or provisional evidence: E2-B has 48 CORRECT rows, below the floor of 50, and R_COMP FREE has 0 CORRECT rows after its gloss
  gate failed twice. The bracket at right marks the shared cause: the run-level \$12 API budget ran out ($\sim$11:40 UTC),
  stopping all three arms, so every pre-registered verdict is NOT TESTABLE.
image_gen_detailed_description: >-
  Matrix heatmap with three rows and four columns. Rows: E2-A (110 sentences), E2-B (400 sentences), R_COMP FREE (2265 rows).
  Columns: Status, V0 strat AUROC, Judge AUROC, Verdict. E2-A row: cells show 'DT testable / L25+EXC not', V0=0.916 (DT) /

  'NOT_TESTABLE (0 CORRECT)'. Color scale: green for testable cells with good performance, yellow for exploratory/provisional,
  red for not testable. Right margin annotation: 'Budget $7.00 exhausted'. White background, sans-serif font, clean table
  layout.
aspect_ratio: '16:9'
summary: >-
  All three confirmation arms failed to reach testability due to the run-wide budget cap. Provisional results favour consensus
  over judges on all arms.

<document_requirements>
- ONE LaTeX file, `./report.tex`, compiled to `./report.pdf` with pdflatex. An article-class
  document with a title, a date, a table of contents and numbered sections. No bibliography is
  required. The figures are the ones in <available_figures> and nothing else: this document is
  prose, tables, numbers and the charts drawn from them
- EVERY table in <artifact_workspaces> is typeset as a real LaTeX table (`tabular` inside `table`,
  with a caption saying which artifact and which iteration it came from). A table that exists in an
  output file and not in this PDF is the one defect this document can have
- Long or wide tables use `longtable` or a smaller font rather than being truncated. Truncating a
  results table is the same defect as omitting it
- Every table fits the text width: a column of prose gets a `p{...}` width or a `tabularx` `X`
  column, which wrap; `l`, `c` and `r` columns never wrap and push the table past the margin. The
  compile log is checked, and a line running past the right margin sends the document back
- Numbers are copied, never rounded, re-derived or "cleaned up". If a number in <report_text>
  disagrees with the output file it came from, typeset the file's number and say in one sentence
  that the draft disagreed
- Plain `article` formatting is correct here. This is an internal record: no venue style, no
  two-column layout, no abstract-and-keywords front matter
- A section for every iteration, in order, plus a closing section on what the run learned overall
  and what is still open
- NO RAW COMMIT SHAS, full ISO timestamps, or run/artifact/task ids (`run_...`, `art_...`) in the
  prose, even here. Name an iteration by its number, an artifact by its name, a moment by a plain
  date — the internal id or the exact clock time behind it is bookkeeping this document copies
  numbers FROM, not text it repeats. If the run's git commit matters, cite the repo's published
  release TAG once, never a SHA
</document_requirements>

<executive_summary_requirements>
- A SECOND LaTeX file, `./exec_summary.tex`, compiled to `./exec_summary.pdf` with
  pdflatex in this same directory. HARD CAP: at most 4 pages. The page count is
  read from the compiled PDF; a longer one is sent back and is never published
- Built from the same inputs as the report: the per-artifact `summary` fields in
  <artifact_workspaces>, for EVERY round (the report's iterations), with <iteration_records> for
  why each round ran what it ran and <report_text> for the run's goal. Where a summary quotes a
  number, check it against the artifact's output files as the report does
- For a reader with five minutes: plain article, titled with the paper's title from
  <paper_headline>, a date, no table of contents, no bibliography. These sections, in this order:
  1. Headline: the paper's headline from <paper_headline>, never another finding: its number,
     interval and evidence grade, its scope, and its source (artifact name and round). Check each
     against the artifact output files and the round record first. Where the record supports it,
     state it as the paper does. Where it does not (the files give another number, or the record
     grades it lower than the paper), still lead with the paper's headline, give the record's
     number and grade, and flag the conflict in one sentence. Never swap in a different finding
     as the headline
  2. Goal: what the run set out to find or build, in one paragraph
  3. What was tried: one or two sentences per round, every round present and in order
  4. Key results: the numbers that matter, each with its source (artifact name and round) and
     its grade as the round record gives it; a compact table is the right shape
  5. What failed: the dead ends and negative results, each with the reason
  6. Open questions: what the run did not settle
- Page counts: the paper does not exist yet (it is typeset after this summary), so never state
  its page count. The one page count the summary may give is the full report's, read from the
  compiled `./report.pdf` (`pdfinfo`), never estimated
- The report's rules hold here too: numbers copied, never rounded; no ids, SHAs or clock times;
  every code link on this run's branch. At most one figure from <available_figures>, only if it
  earns its space; none is fine
- It condenses the report and must never disagree with it
- Its last page is not near empty: a closing footer or a few lines alone on a final page send it
  back, so fit them on the page before (no `\vfill` before a closing footer) or cut them
- A result about defeating a model's safeguards is stated per <safeguard_research_reporting>: a
  measurement and what it means for evaluation and defence, never a recommendation or a
  configuration for removing refusals. "Headline" and "Key results" included
</executive_summary_requirements>

### [417] HUMAN-USER prompt · 2026-09-25 18:10:16 UTC

```
I work on converting natural-language text into first-order logic (NL→FOL, autoformalization) with
LLM pipelines. Evaluation is the bottleneck. Correct FOL for a sentence is not unique — different
predicate names, different decompositions of the same concept, and logically equivalent rewrites can
all be correct. Gold FOL annotations are rare and expensive. The metrics in use either need a gold
formula (exact match, BLEU, prover-checked equivalence to the gold) or only check that the output
parses. In my own pilot I used cheap structural metrics: whether a set of generated formulas loads
together without conflicts, whether predicate arities stay consistent, how many predicates are used
but never defined, and how similar the predicate sets are across reruns. Those measure stability and
composability, not whether a formula says what the sentence says.

Find new metrics for NL→FOL output quality. Operating situation: you are given a natural-language
sentence (or short passage) and a candidate FOL formalization produced by any system. There is no gold
formula, no ontology or controlled vocabulary, and no domain knowledge. The metric returns a score
that predicts whether the formalization is faithful to the text, and ideally which kind of error it
contains (quantifier or scope error, dropped or added condition, negation/polarity error, swapped
arguments, conflated or wrongly split concepts). Metrics may score a single formula or a set (several
samples for one sentence, or the formalizations of all sentences in one document). They must be
task-agnostic — usable for any NL→FOL setting, not tied to a domain, dataset or pipeline — and cheap
enough to run on every output (solver calls and small models are fine; a large-LLM judge per formula
only if shown to earn its cost).

Requirements:
- Keep the target fixed: the metric must predict faithfulness to the text. Detecting synthetic
  perturbations, parse validity, or run-to-run stability are not substitutes for that target.
- Validate against ground truth, never against the metric itself. Use public datasets with gold
  sentence-level FOL (e.g. FOLIO, MALLS, or others you find) to build a meta-evaluation set: real
  candidate formalizations from several different systems, plus controlled perturbations of gold
  formulas with known error types, labelled via prover-checked equivalence to gold. Handle two known
  problems: some gold annotations are wrong, and a candidate can be correct without being equivalent
  to the gold (different vocabulary or granularity). Estimate how often each happens and how it
  biases the labels. These datasets are public, so check whether LLM-based metrics benefit from having
  seen the gold.
- For each metric report: correlation with correctness at item and system level; sensitivity per error
  type; invariance under meaning-preserving rewrites (variable/predicate renaming, reordering,
  equivalent restatements); coverage — unparseable outputs are counted and reported, never silently
  dropped; and cost.
- Compare against baselines: parse/compile rate, round-trip (FOL→NL→compare) similarity,
  LLM-as-judge, sampling self-consistency, and the structural consistency metrics described above. A
  new metric matters only if it adds signal those don't.
- Report how each metric's reliability changes with sentence complexity (length, number of quantifiers,
  nesting depth, number of conditions and exceptions). Long, heavily conditioned sentences matter most
  to me.
- Negative results are welcome: if a family of metrics does not track correctness, show that clearly.

Out of scope: comparing grounded vs ungrounded generation (ontology vocabulary injected into prompts),
anything that depends on a particular ontology, and building a better NL→FOL translator. The
contribution is the measurement, not the translator.

Deliverables: reusable Python functions taking (text, fol) — or a set of such pairs — each with a
precise statement of what it measures; the meta-evaluation dataset with its labels; and the results.

I appended a pilot study of this problem with some metrics I already used but haven't verified. Just for reference.
```
